name: Distributed Cache
tagline: From a map in one process to a sharded, multi-region cache that survives a stampede
summary: A cache trades staleness for latency, and every step of building one is an argument about how much staleness is acceptable and who pays when the cache is wrong or missing. The first version is a dictionary in the process and takes five minutes. It becomes a distributed-systems problem as soon as there are several servers that must agree on what is cached, as soon as the working set outgrows one machine's memory, and above all as soon as the cache is load-bearing — because then a mass expiry, a single hot key or a missed invalidation stops being a performance issue and becomes an outage. Each step keeps the previous design and changes only what the new scale demands, and the three things that actually break caches in production — hot keys, stampedes and invalidation — are argued where they first appear.
requirements: Reads of hot data complete in under 1 ms at p99 as measured by the application, including the network hop to the cache.
Hit ratio above 90% on the read-heavy endpoints once warm, with hit ratio, evictions and key-space size visible per node.
Staleness is bounded and explicit for every entry: a TTL, an explicit invalidation on write, or both — never 'until someone notices'.
Losing any single cache node degrades latency, not availability: misses fall through to the database and the application keeps serving.
A cold start or a mass expiry must not push more than a defined multiple of steady-state read load onto the database.
A working set larger than one machine's memory can be held by adding nodes, without flushing what is already cached.
No single key or tenant can saturate one node while the rest of the cluster sits idle.

steps.title: An in-process map
steps.scale: 1 app server · a few thousand requests per minute
steps.problem: Nothing has broken yet — this is the starting point. One query dominates the profile: a product lookup that runs on every page, costs 40 ms, and returns data that changes a few times a day. The cheapest possible fix is to remember the answer inside the process.
steps.why: An in-process map with a size bound and a per-entry TTL is the fastest cache that exists: a lookup is a pointer dereference with no serialization and no network, so it costs tens of nanoseconds rather than the 0.3-1 ms a remote cache would. For one server this is the correct design, and reaching for Redis here would add a dependency and a network hop for no benefit. The limits define every later step. The cache dies with the process, so every deploy starts cold and every restart sends a burst of traffic to the database. Its size competes with the application's own heap, and an unbounded map is a memory leak with a nicer name — so an LRU bound and a TTL are mandatory from the first line. Staleness is whatever the TTL allows, with no way to invalidate early: if a price changes, the old value is served until it expires. And there is no coordination, which is fine with exactly one process and becomes the reason for step 2 the moment there are two.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Requests the same handful of popular resources far more often than the long tail — the skew that makes caching work at all.

nodes.label: App Server
nodes.why: Checks the map first; on a miss it queries the database, stores the result with a TTL and returns it. This is cache-aside, written by hand.

nodes.label: In-process LRU map
nodes.why: Nanosecond lookups with no serialization. Must be bounded by size and TTL or it becomes a memory leak that competes with the application heap.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: The 40 ms query the cache exists to avoid. Every process restart sends the full read load back here until the map refills.

steps.title: A shared Redis with cache-aside
steps.problem: Scaling out to six app servers broke the cache in four ways. Each process kept its own copy, so the same product was cached six times and effective memory was a sixth of what the bill suggested. Hit ratio collapsed because a user's second request landed on a different server with a cold entry. Two servers could hold different versions of the same row, so the same page showed a different price depending on which server answered. And a rolling deploy flushed all six caches at once, sending the whole read load at the database.
steps.why: The cache moves out of the processes into one shared Redis that every app server reads. The immediate wins are a single copy per key instead of one per process, a hit ratio that no longer depends on which server the load balancer picked, and a cache that survives deploys because it is not in the deployed artifact. The pattern stays cache-aside: the application checks Redis, on a miss reads the database, writes the value back with a TTL, and returns it. Cache-aside is chosen over write-through because it only caches what is actually read (the working set, not the whole table) and because it keeps the cache off the write path, so a cache outage cannot fail a write; the price is that the first read of any key always misses, and that a write must either invalidate or wait for the TTL. Redis over Memcached is not a performance argument at this scale — both are far faster than needed — but Redis's atomic operations, TTL introspection and Pub/Sub become load-bearing in later steps. The costs are real and worth stating: a network hop now sits in the read path, adding roughly 0.3-1 ms and a serialization cost, so very hot tiny values are actually slower than the in-process map was; Redis becomes a component every request depends on, which forces an explicit failure policy (on a Redis timeout, fall through to the database and serve — degrade in latency, not availability); and correctness now depends on invalidation, because a stale entry is shared by every server rather than one. Invalidation starts simple here — delete the key inside the same transaction-commit path as the write — and its harder cases are the subject of step 5.

nodes.label: Client
nodes.why: Sees one hostname; has no idea which server or cache answers.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Spreads a single user's requests over all servers, which is exactly why per-process caches stopped paying off.

nodes.label: App Server 1
nodes.why: GET from Redis; on a miss, query, SET with TTL, return. On a Redis timeout it skips the cache rather than failing the request.

nodes.label: App Server N
nodes.why: Identical logic. Because the cache is shared, adding servers now increases hit ratio instead of fragmenting it.

nodes.label: Cache-aside + invalidate
nodes.why: One library used by every server: key naming, TTL per entity type, and a delete-on-write hook so a change does not wait out the TTL.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: One copy of each key for the whole fleet, surviving deploys. Atomic commands and TTL introspection are what later steps build stampede protection on.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Still absorbs every miss, so its capacity sets the ceiling on how badly the cache is allowed to fail.

steps.title: Replication for read scale and failover
steps.scale: 20 app servers · 500,000 users · 200,000 cache reads per second
steps.problem: Two failures, both about the single node. Read throughput hit the ceiling of one Redis process — commands are executed on a single thread, so one instance could not serve the fleet, and p99 latency began climbing as the command queue grew. Worse, when that instance was restarted for a version upgrade the entire cache disappeared, every request missed, and the database took the full read load and fell over; the outage lasted longer than the restart because the cache had to refill under saturation. A cache the application cannot run without needs an availability story.
steps.why: One primary handles writes and invalidations; several asynchronous replicas serve reads, and the client library routes read commands to a replica and writes to the primary. That multiplies read capacity roughly linearly with replicas and, more importantly, means losing a node no longer empties the cache. A monitoring quorum (Sentinel, or the managed equivalent) watches the primary and promotes a replica automatically, so a node failure costs a few seconds of write errors rather than a full cold start. The trade-off is now explicit: replication is asynchronous, so a read served by a replica may return a value the primary has already deleted. For cached data this is usually acceptable — a few hundred milliseconds of extra staleness on top of a TTL measured in minutes — but it is not acceptable for anything that must read its own write, so session data, counters and idempotency keys stay pinned to the primary. That per-entry decision is the design work here, not the replication itself. Replication also does nothing for two problems it is often mistaken for: it does not increase total memory, because every replica holds the same full dataset, and it does not help write throughput, because every write still funnels through one primary. Those are step 4's problems. What it does add is a cheap answer to cold starts — enabling persistence on one replica means a restarted node reloads a warm dataset instead of an empty one, at the cost of fork and disk I/O on that node. Costs: more nodes to run and patch, a client that must understand read/write splitting, replication lag as a new metric to alert on, and a failover window during which writes and invalidations are rejected.

nodes.label: App Server 1
nodes.why: Sends GETs to a replica and DELs/SETs to the primary; pins read-your-write keys such as sessions to the primary.

nodes.label: App Server N
nodes.why: Same routing logic in the shared client library so the policy is not re-implemented per service.

nodes.label: Redis primary
nodes.why: Single writer keeps ordering simple; it is still the bottleneck for writes, which is what step 4 exists to fix.

nodes.label: Replica 1 (reads)
nodes.why: Asynchronous copy: multiplies read throughput at the price of serving values the primary may already have invalidated.

nodes.label: Replica 2 (persistent)
nodes.why: Snapshots to disk so a restarted node reloads a warm dataset instead of starting empty and triggering a stampede.

nodes.label: Sentinel quorum
nodes.why: Automatic failover turns a node loss into seconds of write errors rather than a cold cache and a database outage.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: The reason availability matters: the database is sized for steady-state misses, not for the whole read load arriving at once.

steps.title: A sharded cluster with consistent hashing
steps.scale: 100 app servers · 5,000,000 users · 500 GB working set
steps.problem: Three ceilings arrived together. The working set outgrew one machine's memory, and because every replica holds the full dataset, replication could not help — evictions began throwing out entries that were still hot and the hit ratio fell below the requirement. Write and invalidation traffic saturated the single primary. And an operator's attempt to add capacity made it worse: the client hashed keys with `hash(key) % N`, so changing N remapped almost every key at once, the cluster served a near-total miss storm, and the database went down for eleven minutes. Separately, one celebrity product page concentrated 30% of all reads onto whichever node owned that key, leaving it at 100% CPU while its neighbours idled.
steps.why: The cache becomes a set of shards, each owning a slice of the key space and each with its own replicas. The mapping must be stable under membership change, which rules out modulo hashing: consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring so adding a node moves only roughly 1/N of the keys, and virtual nodes (many ring positions per physical node) keep the slices even instead of leaving one node with a disproportionate arc. Redis Cluster implements the same idea with a fixed 16,384 hash slots assigned to shards, which has the practical advantage that slots can be migrated live and the client can be told exactly where a key lives; the cost is that multi-key commands only work within one slot, so anything that must be read together needs a hash tag to force co-location. Either way, total memory and write throughput now grow by adding shards, which is what neither of the previous steps could do. Hot keys are a separate problem that sharding cannot solve, because a single key is by definition one slot on one node — adding shards does not split it. Three mitigations, usually combined: a small in-process near cache in front of the cluster with a very short TTL (one to five seconds), which absorbs the overwhelming majority of reads for a genuinely hot key at the price of that much extra staleness; key splitting, storing N copies of the hot value under suffixed keys and having each client read a random one, which spreads the load across shards at the price of N invalidations; and read replicas for the hot shard specifically. Detecting hot keys at all requires sampling, so per-key request counters or the cluster's own hot-key reporting become part of the design rather than an afterthought. Costs: the client library is now cluster-aware and must handle redirections and resharding, resharding briefly increases misses for the slots in flight, multi-key and transaction semantics are restricted, and the number of nodes to operate has grown by an order of magnitude.

nodes.label: App Server 1
nodes.why: Computes the slot for each key, connects directly to the owning shard and follows redirections during a reshard.

nodes.label: App Server N
nodes.why: Same library; the routing table is cached locally and refreshed on redirection so routing costs no extra round-trip.

nodes.label: Hash ring / 16,384 slots
nodes.why: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes moves only about 1/N of keys when membership changes, instead of nearly all of them as modulo hashing did.

nodes.label: Near cache (in-process)
nodes.why: A 1-5 second TTL in front of the cluster takes the bulk of reads for a celebrity key off its single owning shard, trading a little extra staleness for survival.

nodes.label: Shard 0
nodes.why: Holds part of the key space and part of the memory. Adding shards is now how both capacity and write throughput grow.

nodes.label: Shard 1
nodes.why: Independent primary, so invalidation traffic is spread instead of funnelled through one node.

nodes.label: Shard 2
nodes.why: Multi-key commands work only within a slot, so keys that must be read together need a hash tag to land here together.

nodes.label: Per-shard replicas
nodes.why: Each shard keeps the step-3 story: a replica to promote, and extra read capacity for a shard that happens to own hot keys.

nodes.label: Hot-key detector
nodes.why: You cannot mitigate a hot key you cannot see; sampled per-key counters drive near-cache promotion and key splitting decisions.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Protected by a much higher aggregate hit ratio, but a resharding mistake still points the full read load at it.

steps.title: Multi-region, stampede protection and a real invalidation strategy
steps.scale: 3 regions · billions of reads per day · 99.95% availability target
steps.problem: Two outages and one persistent complaint. A batch job repopulated 200,000 keys within the same minute, so an hour later they all expired together; thousands of concurrent requests missed the same keys, every one of them queried the database, and the connection pool was exhausted in four seconds — a classic stampede, made worse by all of them then writing the same value back. Second, expansion into other regions put 120 ms of cross-region latency in front of every cache read, which was slower than the local database. And support kept reporting that a price edited in the admin tool showed the old value in one region for up to ten minutes, because invalidation only deleted the key in the region where the write happened.
steps.why: Three changes, each targeting one of those failures. **Stampede protection** on the read path: when a key misses, exactly one caller earns the right to recompute it by taking a short-lived lock on the key (SET NX with a few seconds' TTL) while the others either wait briefly and re-read or return the previous value; combined with storing a logical expiry inside the value, this becomes stale-while-revalidate — past the logical expiry the cache serves the stale value immediately and refreshes it in the background, so users never wait for a recompute and the database sees exactly one query per key. TTLs also get jitter (base ± 10-20%) so keys written together do not expire together, which is what turned a batch job into an outage. The combination is what matters: single-flight bounds concurrency per key, jitter bounds concurrency across keys, and serving stale bounds user-visible latency. **Multi-region** means one cache cluster per region, each a full local copy of that region's working set, read locally and never across regions; the 120 ms hop disappears and a region can lose its cache without affecting the others. This makes the cache a per-region derived view rather than one global store, which is the only shape that meets a latency budget across continents. **Invalidation** becomes a first-class asynchronous flow rather than a local DEL. Writes go to the primary database and publish a key-level invalidation event to a durable log that every region consumes, so each region deletes its own copy; the log gives ordering per key, retries and a replay path when a consumer falls behind, which a fire-and-forget Pub/Sub broadcast does not. Three properties are worth being explicit about: invalidation is eventually consistent, so a bounded window of staleness (typically well under a second, plus consumer lag) is a documented property and not a bug; TTL remains the backstop, because a lost or unconsumed event must not mean permanent staleness; and delete is preferred over update-in-place, because writing the new value into the cache from the write path reintroduces the ordering problem the log was meant to solve when two writes race. Versioned keys are the alternative for entries that must never be stale — embed a version or timestamp in the key so a write simply makes the old key unreachable, trading extra memory and a version lookup for zero invalidation risk. The costs across all three: significantly more moving parts, an invalidation bus whose lag is now a user-visible correctness metric, one full cache footprint per region, and a stale-while-revalidate policy that must be tuned per entity type because the acceptable staleness for a product description is not the acceptable staleness for a stock count.

nodes.label: Client + CDN edge
nodes.why: Static and semi-static responses never reach an app server at all; the CDN is the cheapest layer and follows the same TTL and invalidation rules.

nodes.label: Write path + invalidator
nodes.why: Writes to the primary database and publishes a key-level invalidation after commit. It deletes rather than updates, so two racing writes cannot leave the wrong value cached.

nodes.label: App (region A)
nodes.why: Reads its own region's cluster. Cross-region cache reads are forbidden because 120 ms is slower than the local database.

nodes.label: App (region B)
nodes.why: Symmetric. A region losing its cache degrades that region's latency and nothing else.

nodes.label: Cache cluster A
nodes.why: The step-4 cluster, once per region: a full local copy of that region's working set with jittered TTLs so batch-written keys never expire together.

nodes.label: Cache cluster B
nodes.why: Independent cluster; its contents differ from A's because each region caches what its own users read.

nodes.label: Single-flight lock
nodes.why: SET NX with a short TTL lets exactly one caller rebuild a missed key while others serve stale or wait — the difference between one database query and ten thousand.

nodes.label: Invalidation log
nodes.why: A durable log gives per-key ordering, retries and replay when a regional consumer lags — guarantees a fire-and-forget broadcast cannot make.

nodes.label: Cache observability
nodes.why: Hit ratio per entity type, eviction rate, invalidation lag and near-cache staleness are the signals that predict the next stampede.

nodes.label: SLOs & alerts
nodes.why: Alerting on hit-ratio drop and invalidation lag catches a correctness problem before support does; CPU alerts would not.

nodes.label: Primary DB + replicas
nodes.why: Sized for steady-state misses plus one recompute per key, which is only safe because single-flight and jitter bound the miss burst.

textAlternative: Five diagrams show a cache growing. Step 1: one app server keeps a bounded in-process LRU map and falls through to PostgreSQL on a miss. Step 2: a load balancer spreads requests over several app servers that share one Redis using the cache-aside pattern, with a shared library owning key naming, TTLs and delete-on-write invalidation. Step 3: Redis becomes a primary with asynchronous read replicas and a Sentinel quorum for automatic failover, while one replica persists to disk so a restart reloads a warm dataset. Step 4: the cache is sharded across many nodes addressed through a consistent hash ring of 16,384 slots, each shard has replicas, a short-TTL in-process near cache absorbs hot keys, and a hot-key detector samples per-key traffic. Step 5: each region runs its own sharded cluster read only locally, a single-flight lock ensures one recompute per missed key with stale-while-revalidate and jittered TTLs, and the write path publishes key invalidations to a durable log that every region consumes, with hit-ratio and invalidation-lag SLOs on top.
